crime.value: Theft/con: Beggs is robbed of a suitcase containing $20,000 in hidden cash by a girl working at Lucky's Bar. Question: Was the girl real, or did Beggs hallucinate the entire encounter due to alcohol after 20 years of sobriety?
crime.quote: Beggs looked at the other side of the booth. It was empty. He reached down for the suitcase handle and clutched air. "My suitcase," he said calmly.

victim.value: Harry Beggs: recently released convict (served 20 years), vulnerable due to age (50), isolation, no family support, inexperience with modern society, and sudden re-introduction to alcohol after two decades.
victim.quote: Twenty years! / "Fifty's not old," the Warden said. "Plenty of men get new careers at fifty, Beggs."

culprit_and_motive.value: The girl at Lucky's Bar (revealed as Beggs' own daughter Angela, whom he never knew). Motive is ambiguous: whether deliberate revenge, opportunistic theft, or whether the entire encounter was Beggs' drunken hallucination.
culprit_and_motive.quote: Angela tugged nervously at the strand of cheap dead-white pearls still around her throat.

resolution.value: No resolution provided. The story ends in ambiguity: Beggs confronts the bartender; is thrown out; goes to his estranged wife Edith; and is introduced to their daughter Angela—who is wearing the same pearls as the bar girl. The reader cannot determine if Beggs was robbed or deceived.
resolution.quote: the old man and the girl, and Angela tugged nervously at the strand of cheap dead-white pearls still around her throat.

investigator.value: Harry Beggs himself: the protagonist and victim who must piece together whether he was conned, robbed, or hallucinating. The reader experiences events through his disoriented, vulnerable perspective.
investigator.quote: He looked shyly at the girl, and she patted his shoulder. "Nice man," she said, cute, patronizing. "Such nice white hair."
